cards.title: Virtio-nvgpu: Near-native Nvidia GPU access inside a KVM guest

depth.text: someone built an **experimental way** for virtual machines to **share an NVIDIA GPU** at near-native speed

It forwards NVIDIA driver requests at the **driver level**, so guests use NVIDIA’s unmodified user-mode drivers instead of translating graphics calls. On the tested RTX 3060, frames over about 2 ms came within **2%** of bare metal. But there’s no IOMMU boundary between guest GPU work and the host, so this is **not hardware isolation**.

comments.text: There are roughly 3 ways to give a KVM guest a GPU. 1) VFIO passthrough: host binds entire GPU to guest as PCI device, which only allows one VM to use the GPU, thus you sacrifice your host display too (unless you fallback to integrated graphics on cpu etc). Strongest isolation because host kernel module driver not involved. 2) virtio-gpu: guest sees paravirtual GPU and loads virgl/venus mesa…
Amazing project! But man, that README is just a textbook example of LLM word salad. It's wild how these tools are so incredibly capable at many things, but their writing sticks out like a sore thumb

I'm a guy with vague knowledge on KVM - having only tinkered with it and briefly had a GPU pass-through setup 2 years ago. I suggest putting the 'multiple guests at near-native speed' use-case in the opening paragraphs of the README.
Hrm, something of a lack of discussion about what level of access the card has to the host in the absence of IOMMU-restricted passthrough.

cards.title: Platform-Independent SIMD in Go

depth.text: Go is testing **fast vector code** that adapts to different chips, with a **software fallback**

Go 1.27 introduces an **experimental, platform-independent SIMD interface** that hides differences between chip families and **emulates missing operations**. It currently supports AVX, AVX2, and AVX512 on amd64, NEON on arm64, and wasm’s SIMD instructions.

cards.camps: Two camps: fans see portable SIMD as a performance win; skeptics say Go’s bigger issue is C/C++ interop overhead, and autovectorisation remains an unaddressed gap.

comments.text: https://imjasonh.github.io/playground/palette-swap/ swaps colors in a provided image in wasm, entirely locally in your browser, to benchmark portable SIMD vs non-portable archsimd vs non-SIMD. Portable SIMD is ~11% slower than non-portable SIMD in this case, but both are ~5x faster than non-SIMD.

I did some testing with the experimental SIMD on a project I was doing to make speech-to-text and text-to-speech models run natively in Go (with CGO_ENABLED=0, so no C depenencies), and testing non-SIMD w/ SIMD. I don't have formal benchmarks for that, but I can anecdotally say the SIMD work made a measurable improvement in the performance of the calculations vs. just plain Go. I'm very…

Just want to say among many portable SIMD solutions I’ve seen recently (e.g. Fearless SIMD), this is the first that makes non-fixed vectors like SVE and RISC-V vector (RVV) easier to support. Glad to see they made this decision
This is why I love Go. Nobody was asking for this, but they took the time to do it right and continue to Push go as a memory safe, high-level systems language.

C++ is getting std::simd in the latest version and I am all aboard writing the vectorization with the least amount of intrinsic builtins I am able to. Even if not optimal, it's far better than the scalar ops.

cards.title: Git-bug: Distributed, offline-first bug tracker embedded in Git

depth.text: someone made a **bug tracker** in **Git** that works **offline** and syncs through Git remotes

Bugs move through your usual **Git remotes** with `git bug push` and `git bug pull`, and it adds **no files** to the project. It also offers CLI, terminal and web interfaces, plus **bridges** to import from and export to GitHub, GitLab, Jira and Launchpad.

cards.camps: Two camps: fans like having bugs in Git; skeptics say tickets need broad access or should stay separate from Git.

comments.text:

- have the webui expose a git remote endpoint
- slightly rework identities (and likely root them in did:plc for pubkey distribution, the identity system from bluesky, without being an ATProto…

You can also do code reviews in pure git: https://github.com/google/git-appraise I used git bug before but found I missed being able to edit tickets with a Markdown editor. So I built this: https://github.com/LoumTechnologies/ticketry

cards.title: U.S. appeals court upholds designation of Anthropic as supply chain risk

depth.text: a court **upheld the Pentagon’s move** to label Anthropic a **supply chain risk**

The Pentagon wanted **unfettered access** to Claude for all lawful purposes, while Anthropic sought assurances it would not be used for **fully autonomous weapons** or domestic mass surveillance. The 2-1 ruling upheld one of two designations; another federal court had already ruled the parallel designation unlawful, and Anthropic can seek a rehearing or ask the Supreme Court to take the case.

cards.camps: Some commenters call the designation politically motivated or vindictive; others say it follows from the Pentagon rejecting a vendor’s restrictions, and that national-security decisions deserve deference.
entities: U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia

I have also learned that OpenAI's president is a big maga donor and now I am thinking of…

This is like a pen manufacturer not wanting their pens used to sign drone strike orders, now the military needs to have a special box of pens that don't…

I don’t agree with the decision, but I don’t think courts should be able to easily overturn the federal government’s findings when it comes to national security in a specific decision like this.

cards.title: Allow Carriers on Planes

depth.text: someone wants the FAA to reconsider its **baby-carrier ban** during **takeoff and landing**

The FAA's **1994 study** tested car seats and other restraints, but not **babywearing carriers** or holding a baby on a lap. The author argues modern carriers may be safer than arms and should be tested—or **not banned by default**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say waking a sleeping baby strapped to a parent's chest feels absurd; others warn carriers can cause crush injuries or fail in crashes.

comments.text: There is a deeper issue, in a crash, a poorly secured rigid baby carrier seat becomes a potentially lethal projectile. Worst comes to worst, today, the projectile is an infant. An infant is substantially softer and less massive than a rigid seat containing an infant. For soft babywearing carriers, the outlook is also grim. The kinematics of the baby, adult, carrier and airplane seat lead to crush…

The decision to not require seats is one of the best regulatory decisions I have ever heard of, and I wish this kind of thought process was more present in all kinds of places. The funny thing is that, I bet if it were used more broadly, given the absolutely enormous safety advantage that flying has over basically any other mode of transportation, there would be a non trivial number of other…

One thing you should know is that when it comes to rulemaking, the FAA isn't an ordinary rulemaker--they do the most of it and they're the best in the business. When I went to my intro to rule making classes, the FAA always rolled deep. If you want a change and you want to make sure the right people see your request, I suggest you…

I just flew with a toddler that was under 2 from the mainland US to Hawaii and back. The toddler is just under 2 so he was considered a lap child to fly free. However at 2 the child for most airlines graduates to a full…

cards.title: Using LLMs to trace alchemical knowledge and decode 17th century letters

depth.text: someone is using **LLMs** to trace **alchemical knowledge** and decode **17th-century letters**

One commenter says their attempts at **17th-century handwriting** were a nightmare; others call this a **strong use for LLMs**. A skeptic says the texts’ **hermetic meaning** can never be expressed in words.

cards.camps: Two camps: some call this a strong use for LLMs; others say alchemical texts’ hermetic meaning can never be expressed in words.

comments.text: Modern machines uncovering ancient secrets feels like modern magic

I've been using AI to help with my genealogical research, and it's been fantastic. I am loving pushing the family history back and catching mistakes that someone who many others share as a common ancestor have made.

FWIW, I have tried my best to make the 10s of thousands of books on https://SourceLibrary.org ergonomic for both agents and people. All feedback welcome. To date, it is the largest collection of agent-accessible translations on the web. The mcp pulls texts and illustrations — and the API provides access to the embeddings. It’s free. We are based at the Embassy of the Free Mind in Amsterdam, a…
Great post, thank you! So, let's resolve ancient Near East chronology and determine an absolute date for the sack of Babylon?

Great use case of AI. Almost 4 years after the sensational release of GPT3.5, the best use case of AI is still being a powerful search engine that can gather information from all corners of the digital world.

depth.text: someone made Factorio's **machines and enemies** into **3D-printable models** fans can download and print themselves

The models were **split into pieces** to avoid extra supports, and almost every design got a push-fit version and one with extra clearance. The collection has **15 model sets**, with 65 individual models in 247 STL files.

cards.title: Ollaya – Ollama for open-source, Jev-style decision models

depth.text: someone built **Ollaya** to run open-source **decision models** on your own machine

The page reports a median of **8.1 ms** for a five-question Laya:multilingual request on an RTX 4090, versus **236–276 ms** for TypeSafe Jev's hosted API; the setups differ, and Jev's figure includes network time. The official TypeSafe Python SDK works unchanged with Ollaya's local server.
data: TypeSafe Jev hosted API median latency

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say Laya makes wrong decisions on complex queries; another says it was a drop-in replacement for their Jev API use.

comments.text: Guys I have a real q, what is the difference between an instruct based re-ranker and laya/jev I just don't see it. Edit: One is that jev/laya are tuned to have better probabilities, but a reranker can be fine tuned to do that as well. And jev/laya use RLCD?

I'm not sure what this means for AI startups if their innovations can be copied by OSS so quickly (what, like 2 weeks?). There's "consumer surplus" for everyone, to borrow an economic concept. But we do ideally want some of the surplus to flow to the innovator, too. I know there were precursors, but that's fine - it's hard to have a totally novel idea in such a popular field. I don't know what…

Has anyone actually seen better or the same results with Laya compared to Jev? From my experience, Laya performs significantly worse. It's less confident and often makes wrong decisions with more complex queries.

It would be good to list 1) zero-shot accuracy and 2) latency on the models page . The LLM-based models' latency is probably much higher than the BERT approaches I would assume. Also curious, it seems from looking at the accuracy scores you gave that it seems to be NLI > Gliclass > Laya (for Bert types)? Why do you seem to feature/recommend Laya more - is Laya better in some way?

Laya is pretty easy to set up on its own without ollaya. I just did that and replaced my current jev API usage to laya running on a GTX 970 with 4GB of vram. Very small context window, but for some existing small llm work I was doing, it was a drop-in replacement and it makes me happy I can get use out of old hardware I have running.

cards.title: First Principles Thinking

depth.text: the post connects **first principles thinking** with **small steps** and faster learning while working with **AI agents**

The author says great senior engineers **ask why they’re building something** and what it will do for users, then **connect the code to what’s happening outside it**. With agents, they argue, putting old assumptions aside makes it easier to try things before deciding an old constraint still applies.

cards.camps: Two camps: one side sees first-principles thinking as a useful way to simplify and rethink work; the other calls it a cliche or warns it can ignore constraints and create complexity.

comments.text: Higher order thinking is more important and rare. An aggressive first principles approach often leads otherwise well-intentioned technologists into strategic / ideological dead-ends. Do we do things because it's the "right thing" to do in the moment, or because of the final outcome that will eventually result? The most ideal answer is somewhere in the middle. I am far more interested in the total…

From the blog he linked to: "I’m going to try designing something way more ambitious." This is how you end up with unnecessary complexity [1]. The best engineers don't aim for "designing something ambitious", instead they come up with the simplest possible design. They take something that seems complex and make it simple. Unfortunately that's not how engineers are evaluated [2]. [1]…

I use the whole "first principles" thinking as a litmus test for bad engineers, if you're emphasizing first principles all the time you're probably a bit of a naivie person, to put it as nicely as possible. subtraction is a great skill to apply to a great many things we do and when people say "first principles" this is actually what they mean but sometimes things are complicated and a first order…

I'm really struggling to see how to make architectural decisions with an agent. It's great when you're at a total loss for ideas, but when you already have some of the pieces it ultimately wants to drive all of the thinking and takes over. Then it just feels like you're deferring your experienced judgement. I've seen colleagues lose the ability to reason any more without asking the agent to do it…

cards.title: The Test

depth.text: the post argues tech leaders' **outrageous admissions** are a **test**, and we should **push back**

The writer quotes **Jensen Huang** saying he doesn't know his address or phone number, then argues interviewers risk losing access if they challenge powerful guests. The proposed response is to **push back** and **fail the test**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say interviewers should challenge Huang; others say Klein's role was to explain Huang's worldview, not win a debate.

comments.text: I don't think it's unreasonable to limit a person's total wealth to, say, 100x the median person's lifetime earnings. In America, the median income is about $50k/yr. Both were getting something out of this. Given this arrangement, Klein had a limited ability to push back (well, he could, but that would mean a bunch of future interviews wouldn’t happen). Instead, he left…

glossary.CRDTs: Conflict-free replicated data types: a way for copies of shared information to combine changes and stay in sync.
glossary.version control: A way to keep a record of file changes so people can see or return to earlier versions.
glossary.supports: Extra material printed underneath overhanging parts so they hold their shape; it can be removed afterward.
glossary.push-fit assembly: A way to connect pieces by pressing them together, without glue.
glossary.clearance: The extra space between parts that lets them fit together without getting stuck.
glossary.STL file: A file that stores a 3D shape so a 3D printer can use it.
glossary.FDM printing: Fused deposition modeling: a 3D printer builds an object by laying down melted plastic in layers.
glossary.decision model: A program that weighs possible choices and predicts or selects one.
glossary.calibrated answers: Answers with confidence scores meant to match how often those answers are actually right.
glossary.forward pass: One run through a model to produce an answer, rather than building it one piece at a time.
glossary.SDK: Software Development Kit: tools a company provides so people can make apps for its device.
glossary.first principles thinking: Starting with what you’re trying to do and why, instead of letting familiar assumptions pick the answer.
glossary.agentic development: Using AI agents to carry out parts of building software.
glossary.codebase: The files and code that make up a software project.
glossary.learning loops: A repeated cycle of trying something, seeing what happens, and using that to choose the next step.
glossary.frontier model: One of the most capable, newest AI models available.
glossary.third-party audit: A check of an AI system done by someone outside the company that made it.
glossary.zero-shot classification: Getting an AI to sort something into a category without first giving it examples of that category.
glossary.social engineering: Tricking or persuading people into revealing information or doing something.
glossary.abstraction: When you don't have to deal with the messy details of how something gets done.
glossary.sycophancy: Excessive praise or agreement with someone, often to keep them pleased.
glossary.agentic AI: AI that can take steps toward a task instead of only answering a question.
glossary.litmus test: A way to judge something using one revealing question or situation.
